spans.text: Both doctors start their transactions at the same instant, so Postgres hands each one a snapshot
a frozen view of the on-call table as it looked the moment the transaction began.
In that snapshot, two doctors show as on call.
Doctor A runs a check: 'is anyone else on call besides me?' The snapshot says yes, so A updates A's own row to off duty.
At the same moment, Doctor B runs the identical check against B's own snapshot, sees the same two doctors, and updates B's own row too.
Neither transaction writes the row the other one reads.
A only writes A's row; B only writes B's row.
Repeatable Read watches for two transactions writing the same row
that collision is what triggers a could-not-serialize error.
Here there's no collision, so Postgres has nothing to catch.
Both commit cleanly, and the table now shows zero doctors on call.
at least one doctor must stay on call
was never a fact about one row.
It's a fact about the relationship between rows, and each transaction only ever read that relationship, never locked it.
That gap, reading a condition and writing based on it while the condition itself goes unprotected, is write skew.
